document_check.note: Li M, Wang Y, Kazis L, Weng J, Xia W. 'Comorbidities and apolipoprotein E genotypes of patients with mild cognitive impairment in transition to Alzheimer's disease', Journal of Alzheimer's Disease Reports 2025; 9: 1-10, DOI 10.1177/25424823251353209. Retrospective NACC cohort (June 2005 to May 2021; 1,330 MCI-to-AD, 1,674 stable MCI, 1,556 non-MCI/AD) analysed with propensity-score-weighted Cox models. The cited HRs (1.17, 1.04 to 1.31; 1.20, 1.07 to 1.36) appear in the Abstract (p.1), Table 2, 'Stable MCI and MCI-to-AD' columns (p.4), and the Results text (p.5). Full text read to the References (p.10).

cited_result: Stable MCI vs MCI-to-AD analysis (Table 2, p.4; propensity-score-weighted Cox models): MCI patients with diabetes plus hypertension vs either condition alone, HR 1.17 (95% CI 1.04 to 1.31, p = 0.01) for AD onset; diabetes plus hypercholesterolaemia vs either alone, HR 1.20 (1.07 to 1.36, p = 0.002).
tool_reason: The cited result is a longitudinal association between baseline comorbidity combinations and time from MCI diagnosis to AD in a retrospective cohort; although propensity-score weights are used, the authors state 'We do not suggest a causal inference' (p.7), so by clarification 1 of the brief it is appraised with the JBI cohort checklist rather than ROBINS-E, and it compares exposure groups (two conditions vs one) rather than evaluating a single prognostic factor.

domains.domain: 1. Groups similar and recruited from the same population
domains.rationale: Exposed (two conditions) and reference (one condition) MCI patients all come from NACC, but the sample was assembled by outcome group (MCI-to-AD required at least two AD diagnoses; stable MCI required no AD or dementia; reverters and deaths excluded), the characteristics of the exposure groups are never tabulated (Table 1 describes outcome groups only), and the propensity weights balance age, sex and race only. Similarity of the compared groups cannot be judged.

signalling.question: Were the two groups similar and recruited from the same population?
signalling.quote: NACC data from June 2005 to May 2021 was obtained on 123,071 subjects with visit data, diagnosis of AD or MCI, cognitive test scores, APOE genotype, and patient reported diagnosis of different comorbidities.  /  Propensity score weights for the models of all groups were computed based on patient demographic information (age, sex, race).

domains.domain: 2. Exposure measured similarly to assign groups
domains.rationale: The same rule (a diagnosis recorded before the index date, the first MCI diagnosis) is applied to all three conditions and all participants.

signalling.question: Were the exposures measured similarly to assign people to both exposed and unexposed groups?
signalling.quote: Subjects are identified with a diagnosis of diabetes before their index date (first MCI diagnosis date; Supplemental Figure 1). Similarly, we defined subjects with hypertension or hypercholesterolemia in a similar fashion.

domains.rationale: Exposure is self-reported diagnosis in NACC; medication use is said to corroborate it, but it is not stated whether medication evidence was required or how discordance was handled, and the authors acknowledge the lack of precise diagnosis dates.

signalling.question: Was the exposure measured in a valid and reliable way?
signalling.quote: Although self-reported data can be subject to various biases, including reporting bias that may affect the accuracy of the information, evidence of medications prescribed on a daily basis specific for these disease conditions corroborates the diagnosis of diabetes, hypertension, and hypercholesterolemia in the self-reported database.  /  First, there is a lack of medication duration for the three diseases without precise diagnosis dates.

domains.rationale: A list of demographic, cardiovascular and neurological comorbidities, MMSE, APOE and medications is named as potential confounders (education, a major confounder for AD diagnosis, is not among them, but confounders were identified).

signalling.question: Were confounding factors identified?
signalling.quote: To further control for the confounding effects from the selected sample, we included covariables at the index date which include heart attack/cardiac arrest, congestive heart failure, stroke, transient ischemic attack, Parkinson's disease, seizures, diabetes, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, B12 deficiency, thyroid disease, alcohol abuse, and a cognitive test score (Mini Mental State Examination, MMSE).

domains.domain: 5. Strategies to deal with confounding stated
domains.rationale: Propensity-score weighting with covariate adjustment (doubly robust Cox models) and a sensitivity analysis with different weights are stated, although the covariate sets are described inconsistently (Methods include MMSE and medications; the Table 2 footnote lists demographics and six comorbidities; the propensity model is described as demographics only on p.4 but as demographics plus the diseases in the Table 2 footnote).

signalling.question: Were strategies to deal with confounding factors stated?
signalling.quote: We conducted doubly robust Cox proportional hazard models with propensity score weights for each of the disease combinations to compare with the corresponding reference group within our study groups.  /  The comorbidities were included in all the models to control for potential confounding effects. Sensitivity analysis was repeated in a separate model with different propensity score weights to confirm the robustness of the models.

domains.domain: 6. Participants free of the outcome at the start
domains.rationale: Index date is the first MCI diagnosis, MCI had to precede any AD or dementia diagnosis, and those with AD or dementia at the first visit were excluded.

signalling.question: Were the groups/participants free of the outcome at the start of the study (or at the moment of exposure)?
signalling.quote: The inclusion criteria include age>=65 by the end of the study (May 1, 2021), MCI diagnosis before AD diagnosis or any dementia diagnosis. Patients whose first visit date includes the diagnosis of AD or dementia were excluded from the study.

domains.rationale: AD is taken from NACC clinical diagnoses with a two-diagnosis rule, which supports reliability, but the diagnostic criteria for AD are not stated (the NACC guideline is cited only for MCI), ascertainment depends on the visit schedule, and whether diagnosing clinicians were unaware of comorbidity status is not reported; the authors also note possible discordance between MMSE and clinicians' assessment.

signalling.question: Were the outcomes measured in a valid and reliable way?
signalling.quote: If a patient's record showed a diagnosis with any cognitive impairment (dementia, MCI, or impaired, not MCI) and at least two diagnoses of AD after the first MCI diagnosis (to control for rule out diagnosis), this patient was defined as MCI-to-AD (n = 1330) (Table 1).

domains.rationale: Only the study window (June 2005 to May 2021) is reported; no mean or median follow-up per group or per exposure category is given, so sufficiency cannot be judged from the report.

signalling.question: Was the follow up time reported and sufficient to be long enough for outcomes to occur?
signalling.quote: Dependent variables were the time from the index date to the first diagnosis of AD or the end point of the study (May 1, 2021).

domains.domain: 9. Follow-up complete, or reasons for loss described and explored
domains.rationale: Participants who died were excluded rather than followed or analysed as a competing risk; there is no participant flow from 123,071 NACC subjects to the 4,560 analysed; loss to follow-up is not described; APOE genotype was not available for 37.6% of stable MCI patients (Table 1) with no exploration of this missingness.

signalling.question: Was follow up complete, and if not, were the reasons to loss to follow up described and explored?
signalling.quote: During this process, patients who died or did not have any AD diagnosis before the censoring date were excluded from the analysis.  /  APOE not available 144 9.3 629.0 37.6 128.0 9.6

domains.rationale: Time at risk for non-converters runs to the fixed study end date rather than to last contact, deaths were excluded rather than handled (for example as censoring or competing risk), and no handling of missing APOE genotype or of participants lost to follow-up is described.

signalling.question: Were strategies to address incomplete follow up utilized?
signalling.quote: Dependent variables were the time from the index date to the first diagnosis of AD or the end point of the study (May 1, 2021).  /  During this process, patients who died or did not have any AD diagnosis before the censoring date were excluded from the analysis.

domains.rationale: A weighted Cox model is applied to a sample assembled on the outcome and on future information (converters required at least two later AD diagnoses; stable MCI required no later AD or dementia; patients with a later normal test, patients who died, and, as written, patients without an AD diagnosis before censoring were excluded; age 65 or over was assessed at study end), and non-converters are credited with AD-free time to May 2021 regardless of last observation, which biases hazard ratios. Proportional-hazards checks, handling of missing APOE, numbers of participants and events in the cited models, and a consistent covariate and propensity-score specification are not reported; variables were screened with a random forest without detail. The survival analysis is therefore not appropriate to the data as constructed.

signalling.question: Was appropriate statistical analysis used?
signalling.quote: Patients who had a normal cognitive test on record after their MCI diagnosis were also excluded from the study.  /  We also extracted patients who were post diagnosed with MCI but no AD or dementia (stable MCI, N = 1674).  /  All models were adjusted by age, sex, race, ethnicity, heart attack / cardiac arrest, congestive heart failure, stroke, transient ischemic attack, Parkinson's disease, seizures, weighted by propensity score, which is computed based on demographic information and the diabetes, hypertensions, or hypercholesterolemia disease.

overall: High risk of bias (JBI cohort, review's rule: item 11 is No). Items 2, 4, 5 and 6 Yes; items 1, 3, 7 and 8 Unclear; items 9, 10 and 11 No.
overall_rationale: By the review's rule, a No on item 4, 5, 7 or 11 gives high risk. Confounders are identified and a propensity-weighted, covariate-adjusted strategy is stated (items 4 and 5 Yes), and participants are free of AD at the index date. However, the analysis (item 11) fits Cox models to a sample built on outcome and future information (converters need two later AD diagnoses, stable MCI must stay free of AD and dementia, later reverters and deaths are excluded) and gives non-converters AD-free time to the fixed study end date regardless of last contact. Follow-up completeness and its handling are also inadequate (items 9 and 10 No), and exposure validity, outcome criteria, follow-up duration and the comparability of the exposure groups are unclear.

tool_changed_2026_09_29.why: re-screen under the operator's clarified rules: Rule 1 is not met. The analysis uses propensity-score weighting ('doubly robust Cox proportional hazard models with propensity score weights', p4), but the question is not framed as an exposure effect. The objective is 'to examine the association of ... diabetes, hypertension, and hypercholesterolemia (in combination) with the transition of MCI to AD' (p1). The authors state 'We do not suggest a causal inference, based on our outcomes' (p7), citing work that classifies data-science tasks, which places their study outside causal inference. The original reader recorded this disclaimer and chose ROBINS-E on the design alone; the clarified rule requires causal intent as well. The cited result compares MCI patients with two cardiometabolic conditions against those with one. That is a condition-type exposure analysed as a longitudinal association without causal framing, so the rule requires the JBI cohort checklist. This follows the operator's P-646 decision (a baseline condition and a later outcome went to JBI cohort).
